problemText: Mary Wollstonecraft defines individual education (1792) as "such an attention to a child as will slowly sharpen the senses, form the temper, regulate the passions, as they begin to ferment, and set the understanding to work before the body arrives at maturity" so that a child may undertake "the important task of learning to think and reason." This definition centers education on —
choices: preparing a child to embrace universal democracy, a goal Enlightenment thinkers broadly championed
cultivating a child's senses and understanding so the child learns to think and reason
memorizing religious catechism by rote, without engaging the child's own independent judgment at all
preparing a child exclusively for a specific trade or occupation, without any broader intellectual aim
hints: Focus on Wollstonecraft's own phrase: setting "the understanding to work" so the child learns "to think and reason."
Rule out any answer about universal democracy — many Enlightenment thinkers actually feared it — or about rote memorization or trade training, neither of which this definition describes.

problemText: Wollstonecraft writes, "it is a farce to call any being virtuous whose virtues do not result from the exercise of its own reason. This was Rousseau's opinion respecting men: I extend it to women, and confidently assert that they have been drawn out of their sphere by false refinement, and not by an endeavour to acquire masculine qualities." Her argumentative move here is best described as —
choices: rejecting Rousseau's standard for virtue entirely and arguing virtue has nothing to do with reason
arguing that women naturally lack the capacity for reason that men possess
taking Rousseau's own standard for virtue in men and applying that same standard to women
arguing women should adopt masculine qualities rather than pursue their own form of education
hints: Notice she names Rousseau directly and says "I extend it to women" — she is applying his own premise, not discarding it.
Rule out any answer claiming she abandons reason as the basis of virtue, denies women's capacity for reason, or recommends "masculine qualities" — she explicitly denies that last claim.

problemText: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) proclaims, "Men are born and remain free and equal in rights" and defines the aim of political association as securing "liberty, property, security, and resistance to oppression." Given the actual history of the French Revolution, this proclamation is best read as —
choices: a legally binding guarantee that immediately extended full political rights to French women and to men without property
an abstract, universal proclamation whose practical application still excluded women and the propertyless from full political rights
a purely religious statement asserting that all political rights come directly from divine authority alone
a treaty between France and its Caribbean colonies formally ending slavery throughout the entire French empire
hints: Ask whether proclaiming rights in universal language guarantees those rights were applied universally in practice.
Rule out any answer describing a religious basis for rights or an immediate 1789 change to property qualifications or slavery — neither happened that year.

problemText: Article 3 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) states, "The principle of all sovereignty resides essentially in the nation. No body nor individual may exercise any authority which does not proceed directly from the nation." This article most directly rejects which basis for political authority?
choices: authority derived from a monarch's divine right rather than from the nation itself
authority derived from popular elections held at fixed, regularly scheduled intervals
authority derived from a written constitution ratified by a popular referendum vote
authority derived from a national legislature's simple majority vote on ordinary legislation
hints: Ask what kind of authority does NOT "proceed directly from the nation" under the monarchy this declaration was written against.
The other three options describe modern representative mechanisms this article does not address, not the basis of authority it explicitly rejects.

problemText: In the Jamaica Letter (1815), quoted here in Guillermo A. Sherwell's 1921 English rendering, Simón Bolívar writes that Spanish Americans were "never viceroys or governors except by very extraordinary reasons; archbishops and bishops, seldom; ambassadors, never". A student citing this exact wording in an AP World History response should describe it as —
choices: Bolívar's own words in their original Spanish, unaltered by any translator
a colonial official's report on conditions in Spanish America, written for the Spanish crown
a summary of Bolívar's views composed by a modern historian long after his death
Bolívar's argument as rendered into English by Sherwell in 1921, not Bolívar's original-language wording
hints: Recall which named translator and year this passage's seed attributes the English wording to.
Rule out any answer treating this as untranslated Spanish, a crown official's report, or a later historian's summary — it is Bolívar's argument in a named 1921 English translation.

problemText: Bolívar's Jamaica Letter (1815) catalogs offices closed to Spanish Americans under colonial rule, from "never viceroys or governors except by very extraordinary reasons" down to, in his words, "neither magistrates nor financiers, and hardly merchants". This grievance is best read as evidence that —
choices: the Atlantic Revolutions, including the French Declaration's proclamation of equal rights, extended identical rights to colonial subjects everywhere
Bolívar's central grievance in this letter was religious persecution suffered under Spanish colonial rule
the Atlantic Revolutions drew different lines around who counted as free and equal, not one uniform standard
Bolívar's central grievance in this letter was excessive taxation imposed on colonial trade goods
hints: Compare this catalog of specific offices to the French Declaration's abstract "liberty, property, security" language — these are two different kinds of claims.
Rule out any answer describing religion or taxation, or claiming the revolutions extended identical rights everywhere — the latter is a common misconception this excerpt itself argues against.

problemText: Italian unification (1861, with Rome added in 1870) combined Camillo di Cavour's diplomatic alliance with France against Austria (1859) with Giuseppe Garibaldi's volunteer conquest of Sicily and southern Italy (1860), which Garibaldi then ceded to the Piedmontese crown. German unification (1871) was instead driven almost entirely by Otto von Bismarck's engineering of three successive wars, against Denmark, Austria, and France. This comparison best supports which point about nineteenth-century unification?
choices: Italy and Germany had existed as unified nation-states since the medieval period and simply reasserted old borders
both unifications relied entirely on peaceful federation among willing states and involved no wars at all
Italian unification combined top-down diplomacy with a popular volunteer movement; German unification was almost entirely top-down
Garibaldi retained personal rule over his southern Italian conquests rather than ceding them to the Piedmontese crown
hints: Contrast who drove each process — a mix of Cavour and Garibaldi in Italy's case, versus almost entirely Bismarck in Germany's case.

Rule out any answer treating either nation as an ancient, reasserted unit, or claiming unification required no war — both relied on deliberate war-making, and most 19th-century nation-states were recent constructions, not ancient ones.

problemText: Britain's early factories introduced steam-powered spinning and weaving machinery, concentrating wage laborers under one roof on machine-paced shifts in place of the earlier home-based "putting-out" system. A student who assumes this shift immediately improved most industrial workers' living standards is overlooking which point?
choices: conditions for many workers were harsh in the factory system's early decades; sustained improvement came later, through reform and organizing
factory work was entirely voluntary, so no worker would have remained in a job that failed to improve their own circumstances
the earlier putting-out system had already provided workers with markedly higher wages and shorter hours than factories ever did
railroads quickly eliminated the need for factory labor within a decade of the first steam-powered textile mills
hints: Recall the difference between industrialization's long-run effect on living standards and its effect on workers in the first factory generation.
Rule out any answer treating factory work as fully voluntary, treating the putting-out system as clearly better, or claiming railroads eliminated factory labor — none of those are accurate.

problemText: In the Communist Manifesto's opening class analysis (1848, Moore's 1888 translation), Marx and Engels write that industrial laborers "must sell themselves piece-meal, are a commodity, like every other article of commerce, and are consequently exposed to all the vicissitudes of competition, to all the fluctuations of the market." This claim is best described as —
choices: an argument that wage labor structurally reduces workers to a commodity subject to market forces
a description of factory owners voluntarily shielding their workers from all market competition
a claim that the proletariat already fully controlled the means of production by 1848
a claim that medieval guild regulations, rather than markets, set industrial workers' wages
hints: Notice the direct comparison: laborers "are a commodity, like every other article of commerce."
Rule out any answer describing owner protection, worker control of production, or guild wage-setting — none of those appear in this excerpt.

problemText: The Communist Manifesto's closing lines (1848) declare, "The Communists disdain to conceal their views and aims. They openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions", ending with "WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!" Compared with the era's trade-union bargaining and factory-act reform efforts, this closing call is best classified as —
choices: an argument for gradual reform of factory conditions through existing parliamentary channels
a proposal for small, voluntary cooperative communities as an alternative to industrial capitalism
a petition asking factory employers to raise wages through peaceful collective bargaining
a call for the proletariat to overthrow the existing social system by force
hints: Read "forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions" literally — that is neither reform nor bargaining.
Distinguish this revolutionary call from trade-union bargaining, factory-act reform, or utopian-socialist community-building — treating all three as the same response is a common mistake.

problemText: Matthew Crabtree testifies before the Sadler Committee (1832) that his hours in ordinary times ran "From 6 in the morning to 8 at night. Fourteen hours" and that when trade was brisk his hours ran "From 5 in the morning to 9 in the evening. Sixteen hours". This testimony shows that —
choices: this child laborer's hours were capped by law at a maximum of ten hours per day
this child laborer worked no more than eight hours a day under any circumstance
this child laborer received extra overtime wages whenever trade was brisk
this child laborer's workdays stretched to fourteen or sixteen hours depending on how brisk trade was
hints: Add up the stated start and end times for each period Crabtree describes.
Rule out any answer describing a legal cap, an eight-hour limit, or overtime pay — none of those appear in this testimony.

problemText: Asked whether he felt fatigued after a day's labour, Crabtree testifies, "Very much so", and states that after returning home the family had no time "to receive instruction from them", so that, in his own words, "All that we did when we got home was to get the little bit of supper that was provided for us and go to bed immediately." This testimony is best used as evidence that —
choices: this child laborer had ample leisure time each evening to spend with family
this child laborer arrived home too exhausted for anything beyond supper and sleep
this child laborer received daily instruction from parents after returning from the mill
this child laborer's fatigue occurred only on the days when trade was brisk
hints: Notice the testimony states there was no time for parental instruction, and the child went "to bed immediately" after supper.
Rule out any answer describing ample leisure, daily parental instruction, or fatigue limited to brisk-trade days — this exchange describes the ordinary schedule too.

problemText: John Locke argued that individuals possess natural rights to life, liberty, and property that exist prior to and independent of government. According to Locke, what happens if a government violates these rights?
choices: the people retain a right to alter or replace that government
the rights themselves cease to exist once government is established
only the monarch may lawfully redefine the scope of the violated rights
the violation has no political consequence, since rights are held only in a pre-political state of nature
hints: Locke's theory of legitimate government rests on consent — and a right to withdraw that consent if government violates natural rights.
Rule out any answer treating rights as disappearing once government exists, or as redefinable only by a monarch.

problemText: Locke argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed to protect pre-existing natural rights, while Rousseau argued that legitimate authority comes from a social contract in which individuals submit to the "general will" — the collective good of the community, which could in principle override an individual's private preference. Which statement best distinguishes these two theories?
choices: Locke and Rousseau proposed the same basic theory of the social contract, differing only in the terms each writer used
Locke's framework centers on protecting pre-existing individual rights, while Rousseau's centers on the collective community's will overriding individual preference
Rousseau rejected Locke's specific version of the social contract outright, while only Locke ever used that exact term
Locke argued that the general will could override individual rights, while Rousseau argued individual rights were absolute and inviolable
hints: Locke's theory is built around protecting rights that exist before government; Rousseau's is built around a collective will that can, in principle, override individual preference.
Rule out any answer claiming the theories were identical, that Rousseau rejected the social contract, or that swaps the two thinkers' actual positions.

problemText: Britain combined several factors that together explain why it industrialized before other economies of the period: large, accessible coal deposits; substantial capital accumulated from earlier trade and colonial wealth; colonial markets and raw materials such as cotton; an agricultural revolution freeing rural labor; and an existing network of rivers and canals. Which statement best characterizes this explanation for British industrial primacy?
choices: British industrialization resulted from a single decisive factor: James Watt's steam engine, with no other contributing causes
no economy other than Britain possessed any of these five factors in any form
British industrialization resulted from a specific combination of coal, capital, colonial markets, agriculture, and transport infrastructure
British industrialization depended mainly on colonial raw materials, with domestic coal and capital playing only a minor role
hints: The concept's core point is that multiple factors combined — not any single invention alone.
Rule out any answer crediting one factor exclusively, denying any other economy had access to similar resources, or ignoring domestic coal and capital.

problemText: Before the rise of the factory system, textile production in Britain was often organized through the "putting-out" system, in which merchants supplied raw materials to workers who spun or wove them in their own homes on their own schedule. How did the factory system change this arrangement?
choices: it replaced wage labor nearly everywhere with unpaid family apprenticeship inside individual worker households
it required workers to purchase their own raw materials before beginning any production
it kept production mostly home-based, simply adding steam-powered machinery into individual worker households
it concentrated wage laborers under one roof on machine-paced shifts, not home piecework
hints: The factory system's key change was concentrating labor under one roof on a machine's schedule, not the worker's own.
Rule out any answer describing unpaid apprenticeship, worker-purchased materials, or continued home-based production — none matches the factory system.

problemText: Germany industrialized rapidly especially after its 1871 unification, building heavy industry and large industrial cartels, while Japan pursued deliberate, state-led industrialization after the 1868 Meiji Restoration. Which motivation is most specifically associated with Japan's state-led approach, distinct from Germany's case?
choices: a deliberate strategy to modernize industrially and militarily to avoid the fate of neighboring, colonized Asian territories
an effort to recover territory Japan had lost to Russia in a war fought just before industrialization began
a desire to copy the Ottoman millet system's religious-toleration model in Japan's new industrial cities
a plan to abolish the imperial throne and adopt a Western-style republican government before industrializing further
hints: Japan's Meiji-era industrialization was explicitly framed around avoiding colonization, unlike Germany's post-unification industrial build-up.
Rule out any answer describing an Austrian war, millet-style toleration, or abolishing the imperial institution — none describes Japan's actual motivation.

problemText: Otto von Bismarck's approach to German unification is often described using the term "realpolitik." Which definition best captures this term as applied to Bismarck's methods?
choices: a politics based mainly on idealistic appeals to shared German ethnic identity, avoiding any use of military force
a politics of hard-nosed, calculated pursuit of state power and interest, prioritized over ideological consistency
a politics requiring formal approval from the Austro-Hungarian emperor before any German unification could proceed
a politics of peaceful federation among German states with no role for Prussia specifically
hints: Realpolitik describes calculated pursuit of power over ideological consistency — think about Bismarck's engineered wars.
Rule out any answer describing purely idealistic appeals, Austrian approval, or peaceful federation — Bismarck's method relied on calculated war.

problemText: Italian and German unification combined smaller states into larger nation-states, while nineteenth-century Balkan nationalist movements against Ottoman rule generally sought the opposite outcome. Which statement best describes that opposite direction?
choices: Balkan nationalist movements sought to unite the entire Balkan peninsula into a single new empire modeled on Prussia
Balkan nationalist movements sought to restore the Ottoman sultan's direct control over all Balkan provinces
Balkan nationalist movements sought to break a large multiethnic empire apart along national and ethnic lines
Balkan nationalist movements had no relationship to nationalist ideas circulating elsewhere in nineteenth-century Europe
hints: Unification combined smaller units into one state; Balkan nationalism moved the opposite direction, breaking a large empire apart.
Rule out any answer describing a new unified Balkan empire, restored Ottoman control, or no connection to broader nationalist ideas.

problemText: Pan-Slavism and Pan-Germanism sought political unity among people sharing an ethnic or linguistic identity across existing state borders, applying the same underlying nationalist logic seen in Italian and German unification at a different scale. Which statement best distinguishes pan-movements from the Italian and German unification processes covered in this unit?
choices: pan-movements built their entire political program on rejecting any link between ethnic identity and state authority
pan-movements were led mainly by reigning monarchs seeking to expand their own separate dynastic territories, exactly as Cavour and Bismarck had done
pan-movements succeeded in creating a single unified pan-Slavic or pan-German state by the end of the nineteenth century
pan-movements aimed at uniting people across state borders by shared ethnic or linguistic identity, unlike Italy or Germany's more contiguous unification
hints: Pan-movements applied the same ethnic/linguistic nationalist logic, but aimed across existing borders rather than at a bounded set of Italian or German states.
Rule out any answer denying identity's role, crediting monarchs identically to Cavour and Bismarck, or claiming universal nineteenth-century success — none matches the actual pattern.

problemText: The French Revolution's outbreak in 1789 is generally explained by a combination of causes: Enlightenment ideas about equality and popular sovereignty, a financial crisis worsened by war debts and support for the American Revolution, the unequal Estates system in which clergy and nobility held tax privileges while commoners bore most of the tax burden, and bad harvests causing bread shortages. Which of these was primarily an economic, rather than an intellectual or institutional, cause?
choices: the financial crisis produced by war debt and support for the American Revolution
Enlightenment writers' arguments that political legitimacy rests on popular sovereignty rather than divine right
the Estates-General's traditional three-part structure separating clergy, nobles, and commoners into distinct voting orders
the storming of the Bastille prison by an armed Parisian crowd on July 14, 1789
hints: Distinguish an economic cause (debt, near-bankruptcy) from intellectual (Enlightenment ideas) and institutional (the Estates structure) causes.
The storming of the Bastille was an event of the Revolution itself, not one of its underlying causes.

problemText: The French Revolution moved through several distinct phases: a moderate constitutional phase (1789-1791), a radical phase including the Reign of Terror (1792-1794), the Directory (1795-1799), and Napoleon's rise (from 1799). Which statement correctly places the execution of King Louis XVI within this sequence?
choices: Louis XVI was executed during the moderate constitutional phase, before the monarchy was abolished
Louis XVI was executed in January 1793, during the radical phase, after the monarchy had already been abolished
Louis XVI was executed by Napoleon shortly after Napoleon became emperor
Louis XVI was executed during the Directory, as its first official act
hints: The monarchy was abolished before the king's execution — the sequence matters.
Rule out any answer placing the execution in the moderate phase, under Napoleon, or under the Directory — none matches the actual chronology.

problemText: Robespierre, a champion of legal equality and the abolition of slavery in French colonies, also led the Committee of Public Safety during the Reign of Terror, which sent thousands to the guillotine — and was ultimately executed by former allies within his own revolutionary movement. This history is best used as evidence against which common misconception about the French Revolution?
choices: the misconception that the Revolution's leaders drew hardly any of their ideas from earlier Enlightenment philosophy
the misconception that Napoleon's own personal ambition single-handedly triggered the Revolution's outbreak back in 1789
the misconception that the Revolution was one unified movement sharing a single faction and goal
the misconception that the Estates-General convened only that single time across the whole of French history
hints: Robespierre's rise and fall within the same revolutionary movement is direct evidence against picturing the Revolution as one unified faction.
Rule out any answer about Enlightenment connections, Napoleon's role in 1789, or the Estates-General's meeting history — none is what this specific history illustrates.

problemText: Napoleon's Code Napoleon established legal equality before the law and secure property rights, and Napoleon's conquests spread these legal principles across much of Europe, even as his own rule was an authoritarian empire rather than a democracy. Which statement best captures this apparent tension in the Napoleonic legacy?
choices: Napoleon's authoritarian rule made it impossible for the Code Napoleon to have any lasting influence outside France
the Code Napoleon abolished nearly all private property rights across the territories Napoleon conquered
Napoleon's rule fully restored the hereditary privileges of the First and Second Estates that the Revolution had abolished
Napoleonic conquest spread durable legal principles of equality and property rights even while French politics itself remained authoritarian under Napoleon's own rule
hints: Legal reform and authoritarian rule can travel together — think about what the Code actually changed even as Napoleon centralized personal power.
Rule out any answer denying the Code's lasting influence, claiming it abolished private property, or claiming it restored the old estates' privileges — none matches the historical record.
